title: Emotions & Relationships Shorts · Episode 2
chapters: Grief: what really happens when we lose someone
Emotional labour: when feelings are part of the job

units.t: Emotions & Relationships Shorts. Episode two.
In this episode: Grief: what really happens when we lose someone, The power of touch and Emotional labour: when feelings are part of the job.
Part one. Grief: what really happens when we lose someone.
The famous five stages of grief were never meant to be a map.
Here is what researchers have learned about how people actually carry loss, and why there is no single right way to do it.
Not a staircase.
In 1969 the Swiss-American psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross published On Death and Dying, describing denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.
She had been listening to people who were terminally ill, not to people who had lost someone.
Over time the stages escaped the book and became a checklist, and grieving people sometimes worried they were doing it wrong because they skipped anger or circled back to denial.
Later research has not found that people move through fixed stages in a set order.
Kübler-Ross herself later said the stages were never meant to tidy messy emotions into neat packages.
They can still be useful words for feelings that turn up, but grief is less a staircase than weather: changeable, overlapping and different for everyone.
Grief lives in the body.
People who are grieving often describe it physically: a heavy chest, a hollow stomach, exhaustion that sleep does not fix.
Many cannot concentrate, lose things or reread the same page again and again, a fog sometimes called grief brain.
Appetite can vanish or swing the other way.
These reactions make sense, because losing someone close is a major stress and the body's stress systems respond.
In rare cases, a sudden emotional shock is linked to a temporary heart condition called takotsubo cardiomyopathy, nicknamed broken heart syndrome, where part of the heart muscle suddenly weakens.
Most people recover.
The broader point is that grief is not weakness.
It is a whole-body response to a real and painful change in your world.
Swinging between two worlds.
Picture a widower who spends a morning crying over old photos, then an afternoon learning to cook his wife's meals, then an evening watching football and briefly forgetting.
Dutch researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described this in their dual process model.
One side is loss-oriented: remembering, yearning, feeling the pain.
The other is restoration-oriented: handling practical tasks and taking breaks from sorrow.
People cope best moving between the two.
Laughing at a funeral is not a betrayal.
Psychologist George Bonanno found that the most common pattern after bereavement was not long collapse but real sadness with fairly stable functioning.
People can absorb more loss than we assume, and there is no need to force one kind of grief.
Keeping the bond.
For much of the twentieth century, the advice was to let go: detach from the dead and reinvest your feelings elsewhere.
In 1996 a book called Continuing Bonds, edited by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, challenged that idea.
It argued that many mourners keep an ongoing relationship with the person who died, and that this is often comforting.
Think of someone who talks to a late parent at the cemetery, wears a grandmother's ring, cooks a family recipe on an anniversary, or asks what a lost friend would say about a decision.
Across many cultures, rituals honour ancestors and keep their memory alive.
The goal of grieving is not to forget.
It is to find a new place for the person in a life that continues.
Hidden and prolonged grief.
Not every loss comes with a funeral or sympathy cards.

Researcher Kenneth Doka coined the term disenfranchised grief for losses that are not openly acknowledged, such as a miscarriage, the death of an ex-partner, a pet, or a parent slowly lost to dementia.
Naming the loss helps, as does a small ritual like planting a tree.
Simply saying 'I know this matters, and I'm sorry' can mean more than advice.
For most people the sharpest pain softens over months and years.
For a minority, intense yearning and an inability to re-engage with life persist; this is now recognised as prolonged grief disorder, and effective therapies exist.
This is general information, not medical advice.
Talk to your GP, see healthdirect, or call Lifeline on 13 11 14 if you are struggling.
The key idea: The five stages of grief began as observations of dying patients, not a rulebook for mourners.
Part two. The power of touch.
Your skin has nerve fibres that seem to exist mainly to register a caring stroke.
Touch is one of the first languages we learn, and one we never stop needing.
The first sense.
Touch is the first sense to develop in the womb, and for a newborn it is a primary way of experiencing the world.
Being held, rocked and stroked helps regulate a baby's temperature, breathing and heart rate, and calms distress.
In the 1950s Harry Harlow's infant rhesus monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother rather than a wire one that provided milk.
The experiments are now considered cruel, but they helped overturn the idea that babies attach to carers simply because carers feed them.
In 1978 in Bogotá, Colombia, paediatrician Edgar Rey Sanabria faced an incubator shortage and began having mothers hold premature babies skin-to-skin on their chests.
Called kangaroo mother care, it can improve survival, warmth, breathing, feeding and weight gain.
The World Health Organization recommends it, and skin-to-skin contact is common in Australian hospitals.
Nerves made for caress.
Skin is packed with sensors for pressure, vibration, temperature and pain.

In the late twentieth century, Scandinavian researchers including Åke Vallbo and Håkan Olausson studied a slow-conducting nerve fibre in human hairy skin, such as the arm and back, called C-tactile afferents.
These respond most strongly to gentle stroking at roughly the speed of a caress, a few centimetres per second, and at about skin temperature.
They seem linked to the pleasant, emotional feeling of touch rather than to identifying textures or shapes.
In one striking case, a patient who had lost the large nerve fibres that carry ordinary touch information could still faintly detect gentle stroking and report it as pleasant.
Our bodies appear to have a dedicated channel for affectionate touch.
Touch speaks.
In a 2006 study led by psychologist Matthew Hertenstein, pairs of strangers sat either side of a barrier, unable to see each other.
One put an arm through, and the other tried to communicate specific emotions only by touching the forearm.
Receivers identified anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy well above chance.
Each had a typical touch: love was often stroking, sympathy patting, gratitude shaking hands, and anger hitting or squeezing.
Brief touches can also shift behaviour.
In a 1984 restaurant experiment by April Crusco and Christopher Wetzel, diners lightly touched on the hand or shoulder by a waitress tended to leave larger tips than those not touched.
Hugs and health.
Touch from a trusted person can damp the body's stress response.

In experiments where women faced the threat of a mild electric shock in a brain scanner, holding their husband's hand reduced activity in threat-related brain regions, and the effect was stronger in happier marriages.
In a 2015 study led by psychologist Sheldon Cohen, around 400 healthy adults reported how often they were hugged, then were deliberately exposed to a common cold virus and monitored in quarantine.
Those who received more frequent hugs and had more social support tended to have less severe symptoms if they got sick.
The study cannot prove hugs caused this, since huggers may differ in other ways, but it fits a wider pattern linking warm contact with health.
Culture, consent and need.
Norms around touch differ widely.
In an often-quoted informal 1960s study, psychologist Sidney Jourard counted café couples touching in an hour: very high in San Juan and Paris, very low in Florida and none in London.
It was small, but later research also finds big differences between countries and relationships.
Whatever the culture, touch helps only when wanted.
Unwanted touch triggers stress, and people, including children, may decline a hug.
Asking 'Do you want a hug?'
costs nothing.
Some people, especially those who live alone, older people and the isolated, go weeks without kind touch.
'Touch starvation' is an everyday phrase, not a diagnosis, but surveys link lack of touch with loneliness.
Welcome hugs, holding hands, massage, sport, dancing, patting a pet or a hand on the chest can all help.
The key idea: Touch develops first and is central to how babies bond, grow and survive, as kangaroo care shows.
Part three. Emotional labour: when feelings are part of the job.
Flight attendants smile through turbulence; debt collectors scowl on cue.
In 1983 a sociologist showed that many jobs sell not just our time and effort, but our feelings.
Feelings for sale.
In 1983 sociologist Arlie Hochschild published The Managed Heart.
Her idea: many jobs demand more than physical or mental effort.
Workers must also produce particular emotions in themselves and, through them, in customers.
She called this emotional labour.
A nurse stays composed in front of frightened families.
A funeral director offers quiet sympathy, day after day.
Hochschild studied Delta Air Lines flight attendants, who were trained to treat the cabin as their living room and to imagine a rude passenger might simply be frightened of flying.
Debt collectors faced the opposite task: suppressing sympathy and projecting sternness.
In both cases, feelings had become part of what the employer sells, and so something to train and monitor.
Surface and deep acting.
Hochschild borrowed two ideas from the theatre.
In surface acting, you put on the expected expression without changing what you feel, smiling at a rude customer while seething inside.
In deep acting, you try to summon the feeling itself, perhaps by reframing the customer as anxious rather than nasty, or by recalling something warm.
Later researchers added a third case: sometimes workers simply feel what the job requires, such as real compassion for a patient, so no acting is needed.
Hochschild also described feeling rules, the often unspoken norms about what we should feel in a situation, such as joy at a wedding or grief at a funeral.
The toll, and what helps.
Hochschild worried that long-term emotional labour could leave people unsure which feelings were really theirs.
Researchers describe emotional dissonance: the gap between what you feel and what you must display.
Pooled workplace studies, including a 2011 meta-analysis, link surface acting fairly consistently with emotional exhaustion, lower job satisfaction and more stress symptoms.
Deep acting shows weaker, more mixed links with strain.
Emotional labour is not inherently harmful, and many people find meaning in comforting others.
It is easier to sustain with some freedom over how you express yourself, supportive colleagues and managers, and a workplace that backs staff against abusive customers.
Genuinely switching off during time off also helps recovery.
Who does it.

Hochschild estimated that about a third of American workers had jobs involving substantial emotional labour, and about half of working women, reflecting how many women worked in service and caring roles.
Examples include retail and hospitality staff, call centre workers, nurses, teachers, childcare workers, paramedics, police and social workers.
The demands differ.
Some roles require constant positivity, others composure amid distress or hostility, and corrections or security work means projecting calm authority while staying alert to danger.
Status matters too: workers lower in the hierarchy are often expected to absorb rudeness without responding.
Customer mistreatment is a significant stressor for frontline staff, especially when they cannot set limits.
A term that grew.
In the 2010s the phrase escaped academic journals.
People began using it for the unpaid work of remembering birthdays, organising family schedules, noticing what the household is running out of, and soothing everyone's moods.
This load is often carried disproportionately by women.
Related terms such as the mental load describe the invisible planning behind running a home.
These are real and important issues, and research on the division of household labour is extensive.
But Hochschild has said in interviews that the term has sometimes been stretched to cover almost any chore, blurring her original focus on managing feelings, especially for a wage.
When you meet the phrase, it helps to ask which meaning is intended.
The key idea: Emotional labour is managing your own feelings as part of paid work, so that customers feel a certain way.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Who were Kübler-Ross's five stages originally based on?
Answer. Terminally ill patients.
Question two. What did Harlow's monkey experiments help overturn?
Answer. The idea that babies bond with carers only for food.
Question three. What did Hochschild mean by emotional labour?
Answer. Managing your own feelings at work so customers feel a certain way.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
